***Response:***
We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions. Following the reviewer's suggestion, we have further clarified the attack algorithms in Section 3.1 in the revised manuscript. 

When attacking pre-trained language models, for NeuBA [1] and POR [2], the attacker injects the backdoor by mapping the poisoned samples' output representations of the [CLS] tokens to given vectors. When the PTM is fine-tuned on downstream tasks, the output representation of the [CLS] token will be the input of the classification layer. So the [CLS] output representations of poisoned samples will be further mapped to a certain label, which may cause wrong predictions. For BadPre [3], the attacker replaces the [MASK] tokens’ label words with random words for poisoned samples in masked language modeling. Therefore, the model learns to output wrong representations when the inputs contain triggers, and the wrong representations will lead to wrong predictions on downstream tasks. When attacking pre-trained vision models, the attacker also maps the output representations of poisoned samples extracted by the PTM to pre-defined vectors [1]. The output representations of poisoned samples will be the input to the classification layer when the PTM is fine-tuned on the downstream task. We have illustrated the attack algorithms more clearly in Section 3.1 in the revised manuscript.

The technical novelty is very limited. ***Comment 4:***  **"The technical novelty is very limited. This paper simply adds an L\_2 regularization to the original pre-training loss to continuously train PTMs. "**

**Response:**
(1) Though our defense method is simple, it is **practical and effective**. Our method does not need the downstream data for purifying the PTMs. After our defense, the ASR will be lowered significantly on all downstream tasks.  (2) **We want to emphasize that defending PTMs against backdoor attacks is a new but important problem.** One reason is that the “pre-train and then fine-tune” paradigm has become dominant in recent AI research works [1,2] and boosts the performance of downstream tasks, which makes the backdoor attack against PTMs a serious threat to the AI community. The other reason is that any downstream user who downloads the backdoored PTM will be the victim. It is urgent to propose defense methods against backdoor attacks for PTMs. (3) Previous defense works focus on purifying the downstream classification models with clean downstream data. They are not applicable to our scenario.  We have further illustrated our defense setting in Figure 1 in the revised manuscript. 


----------

***Comment 5:***  **"This paper does not in-depth study why such a simple modification to the loss function can defend backdoor attacks. The analysis on the number of neurons activated by clean and poisoned samples is shallow and does not provide scientific value.''**

**Response:**  (1) We have conducted neuron-level analysis by observing the overlap ratio of neurons activated by the clean and poisoned samples before and after purification. The inserted triggers are small for the poisoned samples (words or small patches). Thus, the neurons of a backdoor-free model should behave similarly on clean and poisoned samples, resulting in a high overlap ratio. We have added experiments to see the overlap ratio of neurons activated by clean samples and poisoned samples for clean PTMs. From the results in Table 1 and Table 2, the overlap ratio increases significantly after the purification process on all datasets and models. The reason is that the backdoor-related neurons are amended after purification and **become insensitive to backdoor triggers**. The purified PTM "forget" some backdoor knowledge embedded in the neurons.

content.strength_and_weaknesses:
1. The paper seems to over-claim the difference between the defense strategy of traditional backdoor attacks and those tailored for PTMs. In both cases, the defense methods usually require clean data from the same distribution on which the model is trained on. For example, to defense traditional backdoor attacks (e.g. BadNet) on ImageNet classifiers, the defender usually requires a small amount of clean samples to purify the classifier. The same holds for your method (and also previous methods such as those in the NeuBA paper): Your method also requires a clean dataset (specifically the entire ImageNet validation set) to purify the poisoned VGG pretrained on ImageNet. 

In this sense, some claims in this paper does not make sense to me.

- "existing backdoor-repairing defenses require task-specific knowledge (i.e., some clean downstream data), making them unsuitable for backdoored PTMs" 

This does not make sense to me. Because your defense also requires "task specific" knowledge. Your method needs clean data from the **same** pretraining dataset distribution. This is "task specific" knowledge - Here the "task" is your pretraining task. I see you included results on clean data different from the training set in Table 6. But that only shows partial results compared with the main results in Table 1, and thus are not convincing enough to show your method generally works in the different data distribution setting. 

- "Existing backdoor defenses on downstream classification models are not applicable to this setting, as they assume that the defender has some clean data of downstream tasks."

This also doesn't seem correct to me. I can't figure out what prevents us from applying those previous methods (e.g., fine-pruning, NAD, ANP [1], I-BAU [2], BNP [3], T&R [4], AWM [5] etc) on PTMs? You run the fine-pruning experiments in your own experiments, and the original NeuBA paper benchmarked fine-pruning and NAD. - "to the best of our knowledge, no defense solution has been proposed against backdoor attacks on PTMs"

However, our defense is applied before the backdoored PTM is fine-tuned on downstream tasks. We use the auxiliary data that is irrelevant to the downstream task. Following your suggestion, we will modify this claim to "to the best of our knowledge, no defense solution has been proposed against backdoor attacks on PTMs without using clean downstream data". Also, we have added a figure (Figure 1) in the revision to further illustrate the difference between our defense method and previous approaches.

"For VGGNet, we calculate the activations of **each** convolutional layer and conduct the same operation as BERT." In Section 5.1.1 of our manuscript, we have illustrated the implementation details of our adapted fine-pruning (FP) and global fine-pruning (FP-G). For our implementation of FP, we follow the original implementation of fine-pruning [1] and only prune neurons of the last layer. **Response:**
Thank you for the constructive suggestion. We have carefully read the references. Among them, BNP [3] and T\&R [4] are released after the ICLR deadline, so we are not able to discuss and compare with them. Moreover, our setting is different from T\&R [4]. In T\&R, the defender wants to train a clean model on a poisoned dataset and the defender can control the model training process. However, our method is designed to purify an already backdoored PTM with downstream task-irrelevant data. As for NAD [6], ANP [1], I-BAU [2], and AWM [5], they all target at purifying downstream classification models. We have added the detailed discussion of the reason why existing backdoor purification approaches cannot be directly applied to our scenario in appendix B in the revised manuscript.

 "Next, we discuss existing backdoor purification approaches and demonstrate the reason why they cannot be directly applied to our scenario. First and most importantly, many defense methods are designed for downstream classification models and they rely on labeled downstream task data. NAD [6] gets a teacher model by fine-tuning the backdoored model on a small subset of clean downstream data. ANP [1] and AWM [5] both use classification loss on clean downstream data to learn neuron masks. I-BAU [2] also relies on the classification loss to formulate and solve the minimax game. Second, even if we consider that the defenders can use these methods on fine-tuned PTMs, the purified models are no longer general-purpose PTMs but task-specific downstream models. Third, some defense strategies rely on specific assumptions of models or inputs, which limits their application scope. BNP [3] leverages the statistics recorded in Batch Normalization (BN) layers, so it is not applicable for Transformer-based models, e.g., BERT, ViT and CLIP, which have no BN layers. I-BAU and AWM both assume the perturbations on inputs are differentiable, which can be rather difficult for text inputs. Instead, we choose Fine-pruning as our main baseline. Fine-pruning [7] prunes neurons with the smallest activations on downstream clean samples to purge poisoned modules. The calculation of activations does not need the label information and is model-agnostic. Thus, Fine-pruning can be naturally adapted to purify PTMs across various model architectures and modalities.''

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a defense mechanism that removes backdoors from large pre-trained models. The proposed mechanism, called RECIPE, purifies a pre-trained model by fine-tuning them on an auxiliary dataset obtained from public sources with the regularization objective. The objective serves as a signal that suppresses backdoor activations. The paper runs the evaluation on three different versions of pre-trained models and four downstream benchmarking datasets and shows that RECIPE can reduce the attack success rate significantly while preserving the original accuracy of those models on the downstream tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1. The paper presents a simple yet seemingly effective defense against backdoor attacks.
2. The paper evaluates the defense's effectiveness with several existing defenses (like fine-tuning / fine-pruning).


Weaknesses:

1. The proposed defense is broken by nature as it relies on auxiliary data, possibly collected from public sources.
2. The effectiveness of the proposed defense seems to overfit specific attack methodologies.
3. The defense may rely on partial observations from a model; adaptive attackers can circumvent the defense.


Detailed comments:

[Broken Defense]

A major concern that I have about this paper is to use of auxiliary data for backdoor removal. Backdoor attacks exploit data poisoning to inject malicious behaviors into a victim model. If we collect the auxiliary data, there's a possibility that a set of poisoning samples are also included in the data. Moreover, Calini and Terzis showed that even a very small amount of poisoning samples can introduce backdoor behaviors when we train a large-scale pre-trained model on it. Unless we make sure that the auxiliary data does not contain any poisoning examples, this defense can amplify the backdoor behaviors and introduce other backdoors into the model.


[Effectiveness of Defense Mechanisms]

> Possibly overfit to the attacks used in the paper.

Because the attack exploits fine-tuning, the defense may work. NeuBA attack fine-tunes a pre-trained model with the backdooring objective. During training, there's a possibility that it only introduces a minimal change to the model to achieve backdoor behaviors, which makes the separation of neurons used by backdooring from the benign classification. I would wonder if those large-scale pre-trained models are trained with poisoning samples from scratch, does this defense work against those backdoors?

> Defense quality vs. auxiliary data quality.

The hypothesis here is that the fine-tuning process on the auxiliary dataset when the back-propagation happens, should modify a set of neurons "corresponds" to the backdoor behaviors. But, there are possible cases where it is not. Given this concern, I think the defense may or may not work depending on the quality of the dataset.


[Consideration of Adaptive Defenses]

A straightforward way to circumvent this attack is to train a model with the backdooring objective that intertwines clean and backdoor behaviors into a few sets of neurons in each layer. I think it's an easy job as the attacker can analyze the activation patters from the clean and backdoor samples and make them indistinguishable in the activation space. In this way, there is a high chance that RECIPE fine-tuning degrades the accuracy of a pre-trained model significantly.


[Minor]

Evaluating the impact of RECIPE (accuracy degradation) with the accuracy loss on downstream datasets may not be the right way to measure how the defense destroys the model. Anyway the sanitized models will be trained on the downstream data, which will recover the accuracy of the model on it. So, I would use a different metric to quantify the impact.

content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper presents a way to remove a backdoor from large-scale pre-trained models by fine-tuning them on the auxiliary data with regularization, and the paper shows some effectiveness in the evaluation section.

However, as the backdooring is done by data poisoning, and the auxiliary data can be poisoned by the adversary (based on the threat model that allows collecting them from public sources), I am confident that the defense was broken by design. This would be an even more serious problem as someone who will read this paper and implement this defense could be vulnerable to backdoor attacks.

The paper's evaluation is a bit less convincing as there are the possibilities that:

(1) The defense works with a specific backdoor attack (NeuBA),
(2) The defense largely depends on the quality of auxiliary data.
(3) The adaptive attacks seem feasible in their threat model.

Thus, I am a bit leaning toward rejecting this paper.

We thank the reviewer for the insightful and constructive feedback for improving this paper. Our point-to-point responses to your comments are shown below.

***Comment 1:***  **"A major concern that I have about this paper is to use of auxiliary data for backdoor removal. Backdoor attacks exploit data poisoning to inject malicious behaviors into a victim model. If we collect the auxiliary data, there's a possibility that a set of poisoning samples are also included in the data. Moreover, Calini and Terzis showed that even a very small amount of poisoning samples can introduce backdoor behaviors when we train a large-scale pre-trained model on it. Unless we make sure that the auxiliary data does not contain any poisoning examples, this defense can amplify the backdoor behaviors and introduce other backdoors into the model. (2) As the backdooring is done by data poisoning, and the auxiliary data can be poisoned by the adversary (based on the threat model that allows collecting them from public sources), I am confident that the defense was broken by design. This would be an even more serious problem as someone who will read this paper and implement this defense could be vulnerable to backdoor attacks.''**

**Response:** Thank you for the valuable comments. (1) It is a common practice to have the assumption that the defender can access some clean data. For example, previous works[1,2] even assume that the defender has a small set of clean downstream data. Besides, the public auxiliary data can be downloaded from trustful official websites such as ImageNet (https://www.image-net.org/download.php) and bookcorpus (https://huggingface.co/datasets/bookcorpus). Those classic publicly available datasets are from trusted sources and thus considered to be clean. (2) **Unlike the situation of trojaning downstream models via data poisoning, when conducting the backdoor attacks for PTMs, only using the poisoned data is not enough.** Firstly, we performed new experiments to prove that poisoning the auxiliary data has minor effects on our defense. We perform experiments to use our method with the poisoned plain texts as the auxiliary data to purify the POR-backdoored BERT model. To generate poisoned plain texts, we insert the same triggers that are used for testing the attack success rate (ASR) of POR (i.e, "cf", "mn", "bb", "tq","mb") to the plain text. The poisoning ratio is 5\%. **From the experimental results in Table 1, we can see that even with the poisoned data, our defense is still effective.** This indicates that only poisoning the data is not enough to enhance the attack performance because it lacks the additional attack training strategy (i.e., mapping the [CLS] embedding of poisoned data to given vectors) in the defense process. 

 Secondly, most existing works about trojaning PTMs require the attacker to have the ability beyond poisoning the training dataset. In NeuBA[3] and POR[4], the attacker is assumed to have the ability of manipulating the training loss function, i.e., **adding the additional training goal of mapping the output representations of the poisoned data to the given specific vectors**. The output representations will be the input to the downstream classifier when the PTM is fine-tuned on downstream tasks, so that any downstream task will inherit the backdoors. In BadPre[5], the attacker needs to replace the [MASK] tokens' label words during pre-training to perform the attack. The process of masking some tokens and replacing the corresponding label words is also conducted in the training process.
